background.title: What it means to evaluate a study
background.html:
To evaluate a study is to weigh up its strengths and its limitations, then decide how far you can trust its conclusion. A study is only as good as the way it was done.

Three questions do most of the work:

  • Cause: did the thing the researcher changed really cause the result, or could something else explain it?
  • Measuring: was the behaviour measured in a way that is consistent and accurate?
  • Reach: would the result also hold for other people and in real life?

Today's first half gives each of these questions its proper name.

background.title: Monday's experiment words, in one example
background.html:
A researcher wants to know if music helps memory. She changes one thing: music or silence. That is the IV (independent variable). She measures one thing: how many of 20 words people recall. That is the DV (dependent variable).

"Music" and "silence" are the two conditions. The people taking part are participants. If chance (a coin toss) decides who goes into which condition, that is random allocation. Anything else that could change the score, such as a noisy room for one group only, is a confounding variable.

background.title: Consistent is not the same as correct
background.html:
Imagine throwing darts. If all your darts land close together, you are consistent. If they land on the bullseye, you are accurate.

You can be consistent but wrong: all darts close together in the top corner. In research, consistent is called reliable and accurate is called valid. A good measure needs both.

background.title: Reflexes: responses you do not choose
background.html:
A reflex is something your body does automatically, without you deciding. Your mouth waters when you smell food. You blink when something flies at your eye. You jump at a sudden loud bang.

You cannot stop a reflex just by wanting to. Classical conditioning is about how a new signal can come to trigger one of these automatic responses.

background.title: Learning by linking things together
background.html:
Your brain links things that keep happening together. If your phone's message sound has often been followed by news from a friend, you may feel a little lift just hearing it. The smell of a certain shampoo may remind you of a holiday.

Nobody taught you these links on purpose. They formed because two things happened together many times. Psychologists call this learning by association.

background.title: Consequences shape what we do
background.html:
What happens after we do something changes how often we do it again. Praise for helping makes helping more likely. A fine for parking in the wrong place makes it less likely.

In operant conditioning, "positive" and "negative" are used like plus and minus in maths: positive means something is added, negative means something is taken away. They do not mean good and bad.

terms.def: IB command term: "Make an appraisal by weighing up the strengths and limitations." In plain words: say what is good and what is weak, then judge.
IB command term: "Give a detailed account including reasons or causes." Not just what happens, but why.
IB command term: "Give a detailed account." Say what something is or what happens, in detail.
IB command term: "Propose a solution, hypothesis or other possible answer."
IB command term: "Give a specific name, value or other brief answer without explanation or calculation."
Give a reason for your answer, backed by evidence (here: details from the study).
A level in the IB marking table (for example 3-4 marks) with a description of what an answer must show to get those marks.
A person who takes part in a study.
One version of an experiment, for example "with music" or "in silence". Each condition is one value of the IV.
The thing the researcher changes on purpose, to see if it has an effect. Example: music or silence.
The thing the researcher measures, to see if the IV changed it. Example: the number of words recalled.
Say exactly how a variable will be changed or measured, so anyone could repeat it. "Memory" becomes "words recalled out of 20 in 2 minutes".
The plan for how participants are spread over the conditions: different people in each, the same people in all, or matched pairs.
A design where different people do each condition, put there by random allocation.
A design where the same people do every condition, so each person is compared with themselves.
People are tested first on a trait (for example memory), paired with someone similar, and one of each pair goes into each condition.
Chance (a coin toss, drawing names) decides which condition each participant goes into, so differences between people are spread evenly.
Differences between people, such as ability, mood or language level, that could affect the DV.
Changes in how people do a task that come from the order of the conditions (practice, tiredness, boredom), not from the IV.
Doing better the second time because you have already practised the task.
Half the participants do condition A then B, the other half B then A, so order effects hit both conditions equally.
Something other than the IV that differs between the conditions and could explain the result instead of the IV.
Consistent: the measure gives the same result when it is used again in the same way.
Checking reliability by giving the same people the same test twice: similar scores mean it is reliable.
Checking reliability by having two or more people score the same thing separately: if they agree, the scoring is reliable.
Accurate: the study measures, or shows, what it claims to.
How sure we can be that the IV, and nothing else, caused the change in the DV.
How far the results can be applied to other people, places and times outside the study.
An idea that cannot be seen directly, such as anxiety, intelligence or aggression. It must be operationalised to be measured.
Whether a measure really captures the idea (construct) it is meant to, and not something else.
Class word: whether the sample is like the wider population, so the results apply to them too.
Class word: whether the setting and task are like real life, so the results show what people do in everyday situations.
Apply a result from the people and setting of one study to other people and settings.
The group of people actually studied, chosen from the larger group (the population) the researcher wants to know about.
A sample is representative when it is like the population in the ways that matter (age, gender, background).
A sample that includes each subgroup (for example each age group) in the same proportion as in the population.
Something that pushes results in one direction, away from the truth.
Participants change how they act or answer because they know they are being studied or think they know the aim.
The researcher's own beliefs or expectations affect how the study is planned, run, scored or explained.
Noticing and believing what fits what you already think, and ignoring what does not.
Class word: the person or company paying for a study influences its result or how it is reported.
Studies that found a clear effect are more likely to be published than studies that found nothing, so the published picture is one-sided.
Clues in a study that tell participants what the researcher wants, so they change how they behave.
Class word: participants act the way they think the researcher wants them to.
Class word: a participant works out the aim and deliberately does the opposite to spoil the study.
Giving the answer that makes you look good rather than the true one.
Class word: acting differently simply because you know you are being watched.
Misleading participants about the real aim of a study. It is allowed only if it does no harm and is followed by a debriefing.
Telling participants the real aim after the study, answering their questions and offering to remove their data.
A participant agrees to take part after being told what they will do and any risks. Under 16, a parent must agree too.
A fake treatment with no real effect (for example a drink without the active ingredient), given so people cannot tell which condition they are in.
The participants do not know which condition they are in.
Neither the participants nor the researchers collecting the data know who is in which condition.
Class word: several researchers score or analyse the same data separately, then compare.
Other experts check a study before it is published.
Research that collects words and meanings (for example from interviews) rather than numbers.
Data that people give about themselves, for example by filling in a questionnaire.
One of the six IB concepts: whether one thing really causes another, not just goes with it.
One of the three IB approaches: explaining behaviour through mental processes such as attention, memory and thinking.
An older school of psychology that studied only behaviour you can see, and treated the mind as a closed box.
Something that takes information in, works on it and gives an output, like a computer. The cognitive approach sees the mind this way.
The ideas and pictures of the world we carry in our heads, built from experience.
The view that behaviour is shaped by causes such as experience, but people still have some free choice.
The ability to choose what you do, rather than it being decided by outside causes.
Anything in the surroundings that can cause a response: a sound, a smell, a taste, a sight.
An automatic response the body makes without learning or choosing, such as salivating at food.
A link the brain forms between two things that keep happening together.
Not chosen: it happens automatically.
Chosen: you decide to do it.
A stimulus that causes no natural response before conditioning, such as the buzzer at the start.
A stimulus that causes a natural, unlearned response, such as food or a Skittle.
The natural, unlearned response to the UCS, such as salivating at food.
The old neutral stimulus after it has been paired with the UCS many times; now it causes a response on its own.
The learned response to the CS, such as salivating at the buzzer alone.
Produce saliva (spit): your mouth waters.
A device that makes a steady ticking sound, used by musicians to keep time.
The learned response fades and stops because the link is no longer kept up (the CS comes without the UCS, or the reward stops).
After extinction and a rest, the learned response suddenly comes back, usually weaker.
A strong dislike of a taste after it was once followed by feeling sick.
A sweetener with no sugar; the rats got sweet-tasting water.
Invisible energy (like X-rays) that in large doses makes animals feel sick.
A treatment that pairs an unwanted habit (such as drinking alcohol) with something unpleasant, so the habit becomes linked with feeling bad.
Attempts to change someone's sexual orientation or gender identity. It does not work and is widely condemned as harmful.
Feeling sick, as if you might vomit.
Thorndike's rule: behaviour followed by something pleasant is repeated more; behaviour followed by something unpleasant is repeated less.
What happens straight after a behaviour, as a result of it.
Any consequence that makes a behaviour more likely to happen again.
Any consequence that makes a behaviour less likely to happen again.
Class idea: people save mental effort by taking thinking shortcuts instead of thinking everything through.
Latin for "and others": the study has more authors than the first one named.
A group that does not get the treatment, so the treatment group can be compared with it.
